Issued at 142 AM EDT Sat Oct 10 2026

             -----------Synoptic Overview-----------

Hurricane Isaias made landfall near Destin, FL earlier this
evening. It is moving northward and away from Central Florida. An
unseasonably strong ridge of mid-level high pressure, with H5
heights approaching 597 dam, resides east of the Bahamas this
morning. This ridge is expected to expand westward over Florida
and the Gulf this weekend, with its axis passing west of the state
on Sunday night. Deep, tropical moisture continues to be funneled
northward from the Caribbean and over Florida in broad southerly
flow. No appreciable change to this setup is expected through
Sunday morning. By late Sunday afternoon, the fetch of tropical
moisture will begin to narrow, likely focusing somewhere over
Central or South Florida.

By Monday, the remnant energy associated with Isaias is expected
to turn east and reach the Mid-Atlantic states. Weak northwesterly
flow aloft forces a cold front through Central Florida. This is
expected to deliver much drier air through the troposphere 
beginning late Sunday into Monday. By Tuesday, total moisture 
values over the state should range from 50 to 75% of normal.

Cluster analysis of the 09/12Z ensemble suite reveals generally
strong agreement in the upper-air pattern over the U.S. through
late next week. A ridge axis is forecast to be situated near or
west of the state through the period. By next Thursday, an inverted
trough may pass through the NW Caribbean Sea, with its moisture
likely to remain just south of the area.

By next weekend, we will watch the polar jet as a shortwave ejects
from the Plains and Rockies. Physics-based members are nearly
evenly split on whether this energy moves into the Northeast
U.S. as a consolidated longwave trough or a weaker, less amplified
feature. A stronger trough would give the best chance for another
cold front to reach Central Florida around next Sunday or Monday.

             -------Sensible Weather & Impacts-------

This Weekend...

Just a couple more days of this humid, unsettled pattern for
us. Breezy southerly flow today and ample destabilization should
prompt scattered showers and storms (60-70%) to develop, especially
in the afternoon and early evening. These will have a low chance
of producing wind gusts of 40-50 mph, occasional lightning, and
brief heavy rainfall. Highs today will top out in the upper 80s
to low 90s. Combined with the high humidity, heat indices peak
between 100 and 105 degrees. Residents and visitors will need to
stay hydrated and take breaks due to this late-season heat. Expect
south breezes of 10-20 mph.

A few showers may linger into tonight as the ribbon of deep moisture
becomes concentrated over the area. This should lead to somewhat
more cloud cover on Sunday. Still, scattered to numerous showers
and storms (50-70%) are expected on Sunday. This activity may be
aided by the approaching front, which is likely to be encroaching
on the I-4 corridor by afternoon. Shear profiles look rather weak,
but moderate mid-level flow should once again support a few gusty
storms. Highs on Sunday will generally range from 85 to 90 degrees,
warmest south. Behind the front, somewhat less humid air should
reach locations northwest of I-4 by late Sunday afternoon.

Excessive rainfall concerns look to remain mitigated by generally
faster shower/storm motion this weekend. Still, those spots that
are saturated and happen to receive multiple storms in a short
period may experience brief flooding.

Next Week...

The weak cold front settling into the area on Sunday will very
slowly drift into South Florida by Monday afternoon. While we can't
rule out a shower or two Sunday night into Monday along the Treasure
Coast, most spots will be dry. The afternoon looks mostly sunny
and warm with highs in the upper 80s. The big change is that it
will begin to feel much more comfortable, as very dry continental
air aloft mixes to the surface; dew points should dip into the 60s.

Drier air remains parked over the state through much of the
work week, leaving us with mostly rain-free weather for several
days. Lows should drop into the mid 60s to low 70s, with highs
staying warm in the mid to upper 80s. By Friday and next Saturday,
some deeper moisture may approach from the south as a trough passes
through the northwest Caribbean. Statistical guidance introduces low
(30-40%) chances for a few showers by that time. As mentioned in
the overview, a cold front may be dipping toward the state late
next weekend, but this depends on the strength of a trough over
the Northeast U.S.
